title: Myopia -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Myopia is the predominant refractive disorder observed in clinical settings and has emerged as a global public health concern due to its increasing prevalence and lifelong consequences. Previously considered a purely optical issue addressed with glasses or contact lenses, myopia is now recognized as a multifaceted biological condition characterized by ocular growth dysregulation, with environmental factors and genetic predisposition playing a role. Over the past 20 years, the field has made significant advancements in corneal topography, ocular biometry, and optical coherence tomography, which have markedly improved the identification of early structural alterations and our understanding of the mechanisms underlying axial elongation. Similarly, advances in evidence-based myopia-control strategies, including low-dose atropine, optical defocus designs, outdoor-time interventions, and surgical options such as advanced laser refractive procedures and phakic intraocular lenses, have transformed the clinical management of myopia in both pediatric and adult populations.

title: Myopia -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This continuing education activity offers a thorough, clinically pertinent overview of myopia, commencing with fundamental principles in epidemiology, etiology, pathophysiology, and diagnostic assessment. This activity subsequently examines contemporary therapeutic alternatives, monitoring techniques, and strategies to prevent complications, including retinal detachment, glaucoma, and myopic macular degeneration. Participants will have a comprehensive understanding of conventional refractive treatment and innovative therapy approaches. Participation in this activity will enable members of the interprofessional healthcare team, comprising ophthalmologists, optometrists, pediatricians, nurses, pharmacists, and public health professionals, to improve their collaboration, identify at-risk individuals, implement early interventions, and maximize long-term visual outcomes. Enhanced team communication and collaborative care pathways ensure that patients receive coordinated, evidence-based care throughout their lives.

title: Myopia -- Introduction
content: Myopia is a refractive disorder characterized by the eye's inability to clearly focus on distant objects, as parallel light rays entering the eye converge in front of the retina. This optical discrepancy results from excessive axial elongation or increased corneal and lens refractive power, with the refractive error denoted as a spherical equivalent (SER) < −0.50 diopters (D). The worldwide incidence of myopia has increased significantly in recent decades, leading to its acknowledgment as a critical public health concern. Current projections indicate that about 50% of the global population could have myopia by 2050, with around 10% progressing to extreme myopia, substantially increasing the lifetime risk of vision-threatening problems. [4] Myopia often manifests in childhood, advances throughout the school years, and stabilizes in early adulthood, although pathological complications may persist throughout life. Understanding the structural basis of ocular development is crucial for understanding the disease's natural history, which illustrates the interplay among retinal signaling, choroidal remodeling, and biomechanical stretching of ocular layers.

title: Myopia -- Introduction
content: Myopia is anatomically associated with changes in the axial length of the eye, which typically measures 23 to 24 mm in adults. Axial myopia results from the elongation of the posterior segment, together with progressive thinning of the sclera, choroid, and retina, particularly in the macular area. Experimental and clinical investigations indicate that peripheral retinal defocus significantly influences axial elongation; specifically, hyperopic peripheral defocus promotes axial elongation, while myopic defocus inhibits growth. [5]

title: Myopia -- Etiology
content: Children have smaller axial lengths than adults. The emmetropization process begins as early as age 2 years, gradually progresses to myopia, and eventually results in emmetropia by approximately 14 years. Hyperopia occurs when the axial length of the eye at birth is 18 mm, increasing to 23 mm by age 14 years, resulting in a myopic shift of 15 D. However, subsequent corneal flattening and lens thinning compensate for this myopic shift, leading to emmetropia. [6] Conversely, children predisposed to myopia have a longer axial length at birth, which supersedes the emmetropization process, resulting in rapid progression to myopia during childhood. Progression tends to slow during young adulthood and plateaus by age 18 years. In a few individuals, the progression of myopia continues until age 25 years. After age 25, progression can be attributed to lens thickening, leading to a myopic shift.

title: Myopia -- Etiology
content: The etiology of myopia is multifaceted, involving intricate interactions among genetic predisposition, environmental influences, and behavioral factors. Familial history is a significant predictor of myopia onset; offspring of a parent with myopia have a 2-fold elevated risk, while those with 2 parents with myopia have an even greater propensity for early-onset disease. [7] Genome-wide association studies have identified more than 200 genetic loci linked to refractive error, involving processes such as extracellular matrix remodeling, retinal neurotransmission, and scleral biomechanics. [8] While genetics determines baseline vulnerability, the rapid rise in incidence over a single generation cannot be attributed solely to heritable factors, suggesting that environmental influences are primarily responsible for the global increase. This relationship is characterized by the gene–environment interaction hypothesis, which posits that people with inherent susceptibility exhibit accelerated development when exposed to specific environmental influences. [9] [10]

title: Myopia -- Etiology
content: Environmental variables are the most reliably recorded modifiable contributors to myopia. Increased near-work activities, including reading, digital device use, and extended academic study, have been associated with an elevated incidence of myopia in both cross-sectional and longitudinal studies. [11] [12] Results from meta-analyses indicate that prolonged close labor correlates with a markedly increased risk of myopia progression, presumably due to persistent accommodative strain and hyperopic defocus on the peripheral retina. [13] In contrast, outdoor exposure exerts a protective influence, slowing the onset of myopia through mechanisms associated with elevated light intensity, retinal dopamine release, and enhanced depth-of-field stability. [14] [15] Results from randomized controlled studies further confirm that even modest enhancements in school-based outdoor exposure can reduce the incidence of myopia, establishing environmental modification as an efficacious population-level intervention. [16] Physiological factors also regulate axial elongation via retinal signaling pathways. Study findings have shown that hyperopic peripheral defocus induces scleral remodeling by altering the expression of growth-regulatory molecules, resulting in choroidal thinning and accelerated ocular elongation. [17] [18]

title: Myopia -- Epidemiology
content: The prevalence of myopia is increasing globally due to demographic and lifestyle alterations. Current forecasts suggest that by 2050,  4.8 to 5 billion people will have myopia, with 1 billion experiencing high myopia, constituting a significant global health challenge. [4] [19] The prevalence of myopia in childhood exhibits considerable regional variation, with East Asian nations exhibiting the highest rates. Research indicates that 80% to 90% of adolescents in China, Singapore, and South Korea have myopia, with up to 20% developing high myopia before graduation. [20] In contrast, prevalence in Europe is lower but consistently increasing, from approximately 1% to 3% in the early 2000s to more than 5% in recent surveys. [21] The geographic patterns suggest that environmental influences, especially those associated with educational institutions and lifestyle, significantly influence worldwide trends.

title: Myopia -- Epidemiology
content: The prevalence of myopia in children aged 5 to 17 years varies globally and is the highest in Asian individuals (18.5%), followed by Hispanic (13.2%), Black (6.6%), and White (4.4%) individuals. [22] [23] Results from one study reported a 20% to 30% prevalence in children aged 6 to 7 years in Taiwan and Singapore, and up to 84% in high school students in Taiwan. [24] [25] Investigators in China found an increasing prevalence, ranging from 5.7% in children aged 5 years to 78.1% in those aged 15 years. [26] In Europe, the prevalence is 49.7% and 37.2% in children aged 10 to 15 years in Sweden and Greece, respectively. [27] [28] In the United Kingdom, the prevalence among adults aged 44 years and older is 49%. [29] The high prevalence in adults has been attributed to the lenticular component.

title: Myopia -- Epidemiology
content: In the United States, the prevalence of myopia in children is increasing, although at a slower rate than in East Asia. Research, including findings from the Multi-Ethnic Pediatric Eye Disease Study, indicates a prevalence of 9% to 20% among school-aged children, with ethnic variations attributable to genetic predisposition and lifestyle factors. [30] Black and Hispanic children generally have lower myopia rates than Asian American and White children, although recent surveys indicate a reduction in these discrepancies. [31] The prevalence among adults in the United States ranges from 30% to 40%, highlighting the cumulative impact of the development of childhood-onset myopia. [32] In South Asian and Middle Eastern countries, incidence is variable but appears to be increasing, coinciding with heightened urbanization, intensified academic demands, and widespread use of digital devices.

title: Myopia -- Epidemiology
content: Gender and age also influence epidemiologic variability. Girls generally have a higher incidence and more rapid initial progression, possibly because of earlier pubertal onset, variations in near-work practices, or sociocultural factors. [33] The age of onset is a pivotal factor in long-term severity; children who develop myopia before age 8 years have a significantly elevated risk of progressing to high myopia, as evidenced by results from cohort studies conducted in Singapore and China. [34] The Correction of Myopia Evaluuation Trial (COMET) study indicated that myopia typically stabilizes between ages 15 and 16 years, with a significant decrease in progression after age 18; however, adult-onset and adult-progression myopia can still occur. [33] The rise of digital lifestyles has led to an acceleration in adult myopia progression, resulting in a change in epidemiological patterns during the past decade.

title: Myopia -- Epidemiology
content: The epidemiological burden of myopia extends beyond refractive error, as the condition is a significant precursor to irreversible ocular disease. Severe myopia markedly elevates the chances of retinal detachment, myopic macular degeneration, glaucoma, and premature cataract development, with risk estimates escalating dramatically beyond −6.00 D. Results from a comprehensive study of European adults indicated that excessive axial length (≥ 26 mm) was significantly correlated with uncorrectable visual impairment, demonstrating that axial length serves as a more precise predictor of future visual disability than refractive error alone. [35] The epidemiologic data highlight the necessity for comprehensive screening programs, early detection methods, and population-level interventions to mitigate long-term morbidity associated with high and pathological myopia.

title: Myopia -- Pathophysiology
content: The classification of myopia is essential for appropriate management. [36] Axial myopia is the most common type observed in clinical practice and is caused by increased axial length of the globe. A 1-mm increase in the axial length correlates with a myopic shift of 3 D, also known as spherical myopia. Meridional myopia, also termed myopic astigmatism, occurs when myopia exhibits 2 foci along 2 axes. Regular myopic astigmatism is diagnosed when the meridional difference is along the vertical and horizontal axes. Oblique astigmatism occurs when the axis is not at 90° or 180 °. The corneal curvature, rather than axial length, primarily contributes to meridional myopia. Lenticular myopia is the third most critical component of the myopic classification. The crystalline lens undergoes substantial age-related changes that can contribute to refractive errors. Therefore, the lenticular component should be examined for any myopic progression in adults. The severity of myopia is categorized as mild (spherical equivalent [SE]:  < −0.50 D and > −3.00 D), moderate (SE: < −3.00 D and > −6.00 D), and high (SE: > −6.00 D). [37] Some study findings have suggested the need to distinguish cases of extremely high myopia (≤ −9.00 D). [38]

title: Myopia -- Pathophysiology
content: Myopia occurs when the eye's optical power is misaligned with its axial length, causing images to focus in front of the retina. The primary mechanism in most instances is axial elongation, prompted by impaired emmetropization, a feedback-regulated process that typically aligns ocular growth with retinal image clarity. Research using animal models indicates that retinal visual stimuli regulate scleral remodeling through local biochemical pathways, independent of central neural input or accommodation, demonstrating the eye's capacity to adjust growth in response to image quality. [39] Hyperopic defocus on the peripheral retina elicits a response that promotes posterior scleral remodeling, leading to globe elongation and the progression of myopia. [18] [40] This mechanism underlies the current understanding of myopia progression and underpins the efficacy of optical techniques used to treat myopia.

title: Myopia -- Pathophysiology
content: The sclera serves a crucial biomechanical function because its extracellular matrix is actively remodeled during the progression of myopia. [41] Reduced collagen synthesis, smaller fibril diameter, and increased matrix metalloproteinase activity in the sclera, leading to biomechanical compromise and increased susceptibility to axial elongation. [42] [43] The choroid also demonstrates dynamic thinning during hyperopic defocus, with choroidal thickness decreasing before structural alterations in the sclera. [44] Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging in humans demonstrates that choroidal thinning precedes daily or weekly fluctuations in axial length, supporting a role in short-term ocular growth regulation. Dopaminergic signaling in the retina has been linked to axial elongation; reduced retinal dopamine release correlates with excessive axial growth and may explain the protective effect of outdoor light exposure, which enhances retinal dopamine signaling. [45] [46]

title: Myopia -- Pathophysiology
content: Refractive myopia, unlike axial myopia, arises from an increased refractive power of the cornea or crystalline lens. Refractive myopia is less prevalent and may result from pronounced corneal curvature, lens-induced index myopia (eg, early nuclear sclerotic cataract), or excessive accommodation-related convergence patterns. [47] Some individuals exhibit a delay in ocular accommodation during near tasks, leading to hyperopic retinal defocus and axial elongation. Moreover, prolonged near tasks and digital screen exposure induce a transient accommodative spasm, which may precede persistent axial elongation. [48] The intricate interactions among the retina, choroid, sclera, and optical system highlight the multifaceted nature of myopia pathogenesis.

title: Myopia -- Histopathology
content: Histopathological changes in myopic eyes vary in severity, with more pronounced modifications observed in high and pathologic myopia. In uncomplicated or mild myopia, histopathological abnormalities are limited, indicating relatively mild axial elongation without substantial structural impairment. As myopia progresses, globe elongation results in mechanical distension and thinning of the sclera, along with decreased collagen type I fibers and irregular extracellular matrix turnover. Reduced scleral fibroblast activity, increased matrix metalloproteinase expression, and compromised biomechanical integrity facilitate further ocular elongation and increase the risk of posterior staphyloma development. [49] These alterations indicate a transition from typical scleral development to a pathological remodeling phenotype. [50]

title: Myopia -- Histopathology
content: The choroid gradually thins as axial length increases, with the most significant alterations occurring in the macular area. Typical findings include loss of choroidal vasculature, attenuation of medium- and large-sized choroidal veins, and reduced choriocapillaris density. Gradually, these alterations lead to atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptor degeneration, culminating in irreversible visual impairment. Optical tomography angiography studies indicate reduced perfusion density in the deep and superficial vascular plexuses of highly myopic eyes, which correlates with decreased visual acuity and an elevated risk of myopic macular degeneration. [51]

title: Myopia -- Histopathology
content: In pathologic myopia, distinctive lesions result from significant structural elongation and tissue degradation. These include diffuse chorioretinal atrophy, patchy atrophy, lacquer cracks, and myopic choroidal neovascularization, reflecting progressive stages of tissue degeneration. [52] Posterior staphylomas (protrusions of the compromised sclera) are indicative of severe illness and generate localized mechanical stress, hastening degeneration. [53] Histologically, lacquer cracks indicate disruptions in the Bruch membrane and predispose to myopic choroidal neovascularization. [54] Chronic microtrauma results in fibrovascular proliferation, subretinal fibrosis, and irreversible macular scarring, which are significant contributors to visual impairment in adults with pathological myopia. [55] These histopathological findings are along a spectrum from uncomplicated refractive myopia to vision-threatening degenerative conditions.

title: Myopia -- History and Physical -- Clinical Evaluation
content: Individuals with myopia generally exhibit painless, blurred distance vision, although near vision is usually maintained, depending on age and the extent of ametropia. Children may exhibit reading difficulties, academic performance challenges, or actions such as squinting or positioning themselves close to screens or the front of the classroom. [56] The clinical history must assess the age of onset, [57] progression rate, family history of myopia, [58] near-work practices, outdoor activity frequency, and digital device use. [59] A comprehensive environmental history is essential, as alterable behaviors frequently influence the rate of progression. In adults, additional symptoms may include increased reliance on corrective lenses, challenges with night vision, or sensitivity to glare (particularly when lens-induced refractive changes are present). Patients with severe myopia may report floaters, metamorphopsia, or abrupt changes in visual acuity, which may indicate retinal tears or myopic choroidal neovascularization. [60]

title: Myopia -- History and Physical -- Clinical Evaluation
content: Parents may report that a child reads books by holding them close to their face, makes frequent mistakes when taking class notes, is unable to watch television from a distance of greater than 3 feet, and has chronic headaches, which raises suspicion of refractive errors. [61] Adolescents often report symptoms of reduced distance vision. A refractive error may cause headache and eye pain. Patients with astigmatism may present with asthenopia, which manifests as headaches, diurnal variations in vision, occasional diplopia, and cervical pain. Frequent squinting or globe deviation with loss of near vision is a common presentation. [62]

title: Myopia -- History and Physical -- Medical History
content: The medical history determines appropriate management. Inquiry regarding a family history of myopia, keratoconus, and retinal complications is essential. [63] Patients with myopia and a family history of retinal complications or keratoconus should be evaluated for retinal disorders and corneal abnormalities. A medical history of corticosteroid use for allergic conjunctivitis in children is critical for diagnosing lenticular myopia or ciliary spasm with increased intraocular pressure. [64]

title: Myopia -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: The physical examination commences with a thorough ocular evaluation, encompassing uncorrected and best-corrected visual acuity, cycloplegic refraction in pediatric patients, and manifest refraction in adults. [65] Cycloplegia is crucial in pediatric patients to eliminate accommodative spasm and precisely assess refractive error. The slit-lamp examination evaluates corneal curvature, anterior segment condition, and lens transparency, with particular attention to early nuclear sclerosis or lenticular thickness that may lead to secondary myopia in older adults. In moderate to high myopia, the fundus examination may reveal peripapillary atrophy, tilted optic discs, a tessellated fundus appearance, and enhanced visibility of choroidal veins attributable to retinal thinning. In adults with severe myopathy, posterior vitreous detachment may occur earlier due to elongated ocular geometry.

title: Myopia -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: The Purkinje images of the cornea provide information regarding phobia and tropia. The Hirschberg reflex is typically observed slightly nasal to the center of the cornea in orthotropic eyes. Furthermore, in the Purkinje images of exotropic eyes, the Hirschberg reflex is significantly nasal to the center of the cornea. [66] All patients with myopia need to be evaluated for strabismus. Exotropia is commonly observed in patients with moderate to severe grades of myopia. In findings from an observational study conducted by the Mayo Clinic, 90% of patients with intermittent exotropia had myopia. [67] Differences in globe size provide information on anisometropia. Eyes with a high number of refractive errors tend to have larger globe diameters, as indicated by greater scleral exposure. [68] In diffuse-torchlight examinations, lower-lid indentation on downgaze may support a diagnosis of keratoconus. [69]

title: Myopia -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: Axial length measurement and corneal topography yield critical structural data. Axial length measurements exceeding 26 mm indicate severe myopia and warrant closer monitoring due to an increased risk of complications. [70] Optical coherence tomography imaging is advised for all patients with moderate to high myopia to identify early retinal changes, such as foveoschisis, tractional anomalies, or early myopic macular degeneration. [71] Wide-field fundus photography may aid in documenting peripheral retinal diseases, including lattice degeneration, paving stone degeneration, and early retinal fractures. [72] Symptoms such as photopsia, abrupt-onset floaters, or loss of peripheral vision necessitate immediate evaluation to exclude retinal tears or detachment, especially in those with elongated axial lengths. [73] A comprehensive physical examination enables clinicians to distinguish uncomplicated refractive myopia from its severe or pathological variants, facilitating appropriate follow-up and care.

title: Myopia -- Evaluation -- Assessment
content: The assessment of myopia begins with accurate measurement of refractive error, generally with cycloplegic retinoscopy in children and manifest refraction for adults. Cycloplegic medications, such as cyclopentolate, are crucial in pediatric assessments to inhibit accommodation and reveal the accurate refractive state. Objective measurements are frequently followed by subjective adjustments when appropriate for age. A thorough evaluation includes distance and near visual acuity, accommodation amplitude, and binocular vision assessment to identify factors that may influence progression. Because myopia often begins during academic years, early screening is strongly recommended; the US Preventive Services Task Force recommends vision screening in children to identify refractive errors earlier. [74] School-based screening programs have improved detection and can facilitate prompt implementation of myopia-control methods, thereby mitigating long-term visual morbidity.

title: Myopia -- Evaluation -- Retinoscopy
content: Retinoscopy is a critical tool for measuring refractive errors. [75] Spot and streak retinoscopy are used most commonly in clinical practice. [76] Illumination is provided by a round filament in spot retinoscopy and a streak filament in streak retinoscopy, based on the Foucault principle. [77] Light reflected from a mirror projected onto the eye moves according to the eye’s refractive state. Retinoscopy is used to locate the eye’s far point (conjugate to the retina), with accommodation at rest. The refractive error is determined using the neutralization technique, in which the movement of the projected light from a preconceived distance into the eye ceases. The standard working distance is 67 cm.

title: Myopia -- Evaluation -- Retinoscopy
content: In patients with myopia of > 1.5 D, the reflected light from the retina moves in the opposite direction to the movement of the projected light. To calculate the refractive error, power is added until the neutralization point is reached, and the working distance and cycloplegic correction are then subtracted (subtract 1.5 D for atropine and 1.0 D for homatropine). [78] (See Image . Steps of Retinoscopy). In patients with myopia < 1.5 D, the reflected light moves in the same direction as the streak light. Neutralization should be performed in both meridians, perpendicular to each other, and well documented. If the patient’s astigmatism is oblique, the streak light should be rotated until it falls along the line of the reflex. Dynamic retinoscopy can be performed during accommodation; however, it is highly inaccurate.

title: Myopia -- Evaluation -- Autorefractometer
content: With the advent of autorefractometers, diagnosing myopia has become easier. [79] Autorefractometers have completely replaced retinoscopy in routine screening for myopia. The diagnostic capacity of autorefractometers is based on the optometer principle described by Porter in 1759. [80] [81] Autorefractometers objectively measure the degree of myopia with high accuracy. [82] They use infrared light with a wavelength of 800 to 900 nm, projected into the eye, and the reflected light is used to calculate refractive errors. Some devices use the Scheiner double-pinhole principle, in which light-emitting diodes are positioned at the objective lens's focal length. Because infrared light is not visible, it bypasses the accommodation reflex. Additionally, some targets incorporate peripheral blur to reduce accommodation. [83]

title: Myopia -- Evaluation -- Autorefractometer
content: Many modern devices also use the fogging method to relax accommodation. However, the accurate assessment of refractive errors in children with hyperaccommodation requires cycloplegia. Results from multiple studies have reported that the efficacy of autorefractometers is comparable to that of retinoscopy. Dilated retinoscopy remains the gold standard for identifying refractive errors that do not align with subjective findings. [84] [85]

title: Myopia -- Evaluation -- Corneal Topography
content: Corneal topography plays a critical role in identifying myopia-related corneal disorders. [86] Patients with high myopic astigmatism require keratoconus forme fruste screening. Corneal topography is essential for identifying patients with myopia who are eligible for laser refractive surgery. Corneal analysis assesses the biomechanical integrity of the cornea, helping surgeons plan appropriate management and provide spectacle-free vision.

title: Myopia -- Evaluation -- Corneal Topography
content: Topography is performed using various technologies; however, Orbscan and Pentacam are most commonly used. Orbscan uses slit imaging technology, in which 40 oblique slits of light are passed from either side, and the light reflected from the anterior and posterior corneal surfaces is analyzed. However, Orbscan II integrates Placido rings and slit images to provide more comprehensive corneal information. [87] The mechanism of Orbscan II is similar to that of a camera photographing from the top of an island; Orbscan II data are converted into a 2-dimensional format using false-color coding. Orbscan provides a quad map or four maps showing the anterior surface of the cornea (anterior float), the posterior surface of the cornea (posterior float), corneal thickness (pachymetric map), and corneal curvature (keratometric map). Additionally, the Orbscan instrument provides a middle box consisting of average keratometric readings from the 3-mm and 5-mm zones of the cornea. Before keratorefractive procedures, topography should be reviewed for findings that increase the risk of ectasia; multiple concerning features may contraindicate surgery.

title: Myopia -- Evaluation -- Corneal Topography
content: With the advent of Schiempflug technology, Orbscan devices have become obsolete. [88] This technology combines a rotating camera with slit lights that rotate like a wheel's spokes for corneal analysis, along with a central static camera to measure pupil size and fixate the eye during data capture. This approach is based on the Schiempflug principle, which states that a higher depth of focus is achieved when the picture, lens, and object planes intersect along a single line. This technique provides information not only about the cornea but also about the angle of the anterior chamber and its depth.

title: Myopia -- Evaluation -- Corneal Topography
content: The anterior chamber depth is critical for implanting a phakic intraocular lens (IOL) in candidates with contraindications to keratorefractive procedures. Moreover, in addition to the quad map, Pentacam offers a Belin-Ambrosio enhanced ectasia display, which combines all corneal information into a single display. Belin-Ambrosio enhanced ectasia display compares the anterior and posterior curvature maps of the cornea with computer-generated maps based on peripheral corneal curvature (excluding the central 3 mm), extrapolated to the center. [88] (See Image . Belin-Ambrosio Enhanced Ectasia Display).

content: A significant difference between a patient's cornea and the computer-generated cornea denotes a contraindication for laser refractive surgery. Similarly, a computer-generated spatial profile of corneal thickness and a percentage increase in thickness from the center to the periphery are created from pachymetric data; the profile line should fall within three reference data lines. Additionally, a reference database is incorporated into the map by comparing each patient's overall corneal information with that of the healthy population, thereby screening all patients with suspicious corneal abnormalities. title: Myopia -- Evaluation -- Slit-Lamp Examination
content: Slit-lamp examination provides general information about the corneal thickness, anterior chamber depth, iridocorneal angle, lenticular thickness, optic disc, and macula. [89] The oblique slit can be used to analyze the uniformity of the corneal thickness. Subtle thinning of the cornea can be identified using the oblique slit, mainly in the inferior quadrant, which should be correlated with the corneal topography to diagnose keratoconus. Thinning near the inferior limbus can correlate with against-the-rule astigmatism in pellucid marginal degeneration. [90]

title: Myopia -- Evaluation -- Slit-Lamp Examination
content: The iridocorneal angle can be evaluated using the oblique slit in a dark environment, with corneal thickness as the reference. A gross evaluation of central anterior chamber depth can be performed; however, quantitative assessment and screening require Pentacam or optical biometers. Lenticular assessment is the most critical component of slit-lamp examination. The cataractous transformation of the crystalline lens may cause progressive myopia in older adults. Nuclear maturation of the crystalline lens improves unaided near vision in older patients, also known as second sight . [91] Slit-lamp biomicroscopic evaluation of the posterior pole and optic disc can be performed with a 90-D fundoscopic lens, which enables evaluation even in undilated pupils. [92]

title: Myopia -- Evaluation -- Posterior Segment Examination
content: Assessment of the posterior segment is essential in moderate to high myopia. A dilated fundus examination facilitates the evaluation of peripheral retinal abnormalities, including lattice degeneration, retinal holes, or thinning, which may increase the risk of tears and detachment. Wide-field fundus photography improves documentation and temporal comparison, especially in individuals with posterior staphylomas or advancing macular alterations. [93] Optical coherence tomography is crucial for identifying early indicators of myopic traction maculopathy, including foveoschisis, epiretinal membrane development, and lamellar macular holes. [94] Recent OCT angiography investigations indicate diminished perfusion density and choroidal thinning in high myopia, which correlates with a decline in visual function. These imaging methods provide a comprehensive structural evaluation that cannot be inferred solely from refractive error.

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management
content: The management of myopia includes corrective strategies to improve vision and interventions designed to mitigate axial elongation and refractive progression. The principal objective of early management is to limit the risk of developing high or pathological myopia, which is associated with irreversible visual impairment. Conventional corrective methods (spectacles, soft contact lenses, and rigid gas-permeable lenses) improve visual acuity but do not modify the long-term progression of myopia. Optical advancements, including dual-focus soft contact lenses, peripheral defocus-modifying spectacle lenses, and orthokeratology, slow axial elongation in children. Myopia treatment can be classified into nonsurgical and surgical.

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Spectacle correction:
content: Spectacle correction is the most widely used management for patients with myopia. [95] Spectacles use concave lenses that shift the focus to the foveal level. A concave lens forms a virtual, reduced image. However, the appropriate prescription of lenses is essential for providing correct dynamics. [96] Additionally, proper back vertex distance and centralization of the optics at the center of the pupil are vital for achieving corrected visual acuity. Patients who are uncomfortable with their glasses beyond 15 days should be evaluated for appropriate optical dispensing. Errors in lens power, cylinder axis, or lens fitting can accentuate blurring and cause eye strain.

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Spectacle correction:
content: Advances in lens materials have expanded options for patients. With the advent of high-index materials such as polycarbonate, traditional lens materials, including crown glass and CR-39, have become obsolete. [97] High-index glasses significantly reduce the weight, particularly those correcting high refractive errors. [98] However, users reported dissatisfaction due to decreased light transmissibility, surface reflections, glare, and ghost images. Antireflective coating applied to the surface can address these issues through thin-film interference, and its thickness is calculated based on the glass's index of refraction (which provides optimal refraction). The arc reflects light from its upper and lower surfaces, whose waves are synchronized so that they eventually cancel each other, producing zero reflection. [99]

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Contact lenses:
content: Contact lenses have revolutionized the management of myopia. [100] Contact lens effectiveness depends on oxygen permeability, wetting ability, water content, thickness, and mechanical properties. Contact lenses are manufactured from malleable, durable materials. Previously, contact lenses were made of polymethylmethacrylate; however, their use was limited due to inflexibility and poor oxygen permeability. Contact lenses are broadly classified into rigid gas–permeable and soft contact lenses. Rigid gas–permeable lenses contain a hydrophilic comonomer, which is expensive and may scratch the lens surface. [101]

content: Soft contact lenses are made of 2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA) hydrogel, silicone hydrogel, and polyvinyl alcohol. Contact lenses made of HEMA and silicone hydrogels have approximately 50% water content, high oxygen permeability, and can be worn for 1 to 5 days. Although soft contact lenses have a high water content due to polyvinyl alcohol, they have relatively low oxygen permeability, so they should be removed before sleep. These lenses are popular and extensively used to provide spectacle-free vision in adolescents and young adults.

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Contact lenses:
content: The power of contact lenses is calculated from the spectacle correction and the vertex factor. The vertex factor is the power added to correct the back vertex distance. The correction factor is lower for eyes with fewer refractive errors and vice versa. The cylindrical power can be prescribed by ordering a toric contact lens. However, the cylindrical power can be nullified by adding the spherical equivalent of the cylinder (cylindrical power divided by 2) to the sphere, and the total spherical power can be prescribed after correcting for the back vertex distance. [102]

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Contact lenses:
content: All contact lenses are prone to complications, broadly classified as noninfectious or infectious. [103] Noninfectious complications are the most common, including contact lens-induced inflammation, ocular surface hypoxia, and exacerbation of allergic conjunctivitis. [104] Contact lens–induced inflammation encompasses conditions affecting the conjunctiva and cornea. Mechanical irritation from the contact lens edge on the tarsal conjunctiva releases chemotactic factors, which eventually lead to substantial local or general papillary hyperplasia. [105]

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Contact lenses:
content: The cornea is significantly affected by overwearing contact lenses, leading to corneal hypoxia and blurred vision that subsides after lens removal. Moreover, lenses produce infiltrates ranging from a single asymptomatic infiltrate to diffuse infiltrates. These infiltrates may be infectious or noninfectious. Infectious corneal ulcers are caused mainly by gram-negative bacteria, particularly Pseudomonas aerugiinosa , and free-water amoebae, such as Acanthamoeba . [106] Hence, adequate contact lens hygiene should be maintained to prevent complications.

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Eye drops:
content: Pharmacological intervention, specifically low-dose atropine, is a key component of myopia management. Results from randomized controlled trials, including the Low-Concentration Atropine for Myopia Progression study, indicate that atropine concentrations of 0.05%, 0.025%, and 0.01% attenuate refractive progression and axial elongation to varying degrees, with higher concentrations yielding more pronounced effects and increased adverse effects such as photophobia and diminished accommodation. [107] Longitudinal investigation findings indicate that 0.01% atropine demonstrates minimal rebound effect upon discontinuation, rendering it a first-line treatment in numerous countries. [108] Recommendations from the World Health Organization, International Myopia Institute, and other national ophthalmology societies endorse the use of atropine for the management of progressive myopia in children, highlighting the necessity for careful monitoring of pupil size, accommodation, and near visual acuity. [109] Clinical trials are currently investigating combination therapy involving atropine and optical interventions, with preliminary results indicating synergistic effects in decelerating axial elongation. [110]

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Eye drops:
content: Orthokeratology has been reported to be an effective treatment, particularly for intermediate myopia. [111] Overnight use of rigid gas-permeable lenses alters the corneal epithelium, temporarily decreasing refractive error and causing relative peripheral myopic defocus. Results from randomized clinical trials, including the Retardation of Myopia in Orthokeratology study, demonstrate that orthokeratology reduces axial elongation by approximately 43% to 50% over 2 years compared with spectacle use. [112] Clinicians must evaluate the risk of microbial keratitis, especially in children; although uncommon, it can result in irreversible visual loss. Rigorous compliance with cleanliness measures and consistent monitoring are crucial to reduce risks. Orthokeratology is most appropriate for children who demonstrate good hygiene, strong motivation, and parental supervision.

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Progressive and defocus spectacles:
content: These lenses have become a significant component of optical myopia control, with the evidence base quickly expanding. These designs aim either to diminish accommodative lag and near-induced hyperopic defocus (progressive addition and bifocal lenses) or to create simultaneous peripheral or full-field myopic defocus or contrast modulation (eg, defocus incorporated multiple segments [DIMS], highly aspherical lenslets/slightly aspherical lenslets [HAL/SAL], diffusion optics technology [DOT], cylindrical annular refractive elements [CARE], and similar designs), to decelerate axial elongation in children. Classic single-vision lenses completely correct central refractive error but render the peripheral retina relatively hyperopic in the majority of myopic eyes, a cue that promotes axial elongation in animal models and is believed to play a significant role in the evolution of myopia in humans.

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Progressive and defocus spectacles:
content: Children with myopia frequently exhibit heightened accommodative latency and near esophoria during close tasks, exacerbating retinal hyperopic haze at near distances. Progressive addition lenses (PALs) and bifocals were initially designed to mitigate accommodative lag and related hyperopic defocus during near tasks. In contrast, contemporary myopia-specific spectacle designs incorporate arrays of plus-powered or aspherical segments in the peripheral or midperipheral regions to generate simultaneous myopic defocus across a broad retinal area. [113]

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Progressive and defocus spectacles:
content: The myopic defocus designs (eg, DIMS, HAL/SAL, CARE) are intended to maintain clarity at the central distance while providing a concentrated pattern of positive power in the peripheral field, thereby shifting the overall retinal image towards relative myopic defocus, which is thought to inhibit scleral remodeling and axial elongation. Diffusion optics technology lenses employ microdiffusers to reduce retinal contrast in a controlled spatial arrangement, based on the hypothesis that persistently heightened fine-scale contrast in contemporary near environments induces excessive ocular growth; reducing contrast is believed to normalize retinal signaling. [114] These optical strategies are substantiated by numerous randomized clinical trials and recent network meta-analyses indicating that myopia-control spectacle designs can diminish refractive progression and axial elongation by approximately 10% to 20% for conventional progressive addition lenses and by about 40% to 60% for contemporary myopia-specific defocus/contrast-modulating lenses, while maintaining satisfactory visual function and safety profiles. [115]

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Progressive and defocus spectacles:
content: The COMET study was the first extensive randomized clinical trial to assess whether progressive addition lenses mitigate myopia progression compared with single-vision lenses in pediatric populations. [116] In the COMET study, 469 children with myopia (−1.25 to −4.50 D, aged 6 to 11 years) were randomized to receive progressive addition lenses with a +2.00 D addition or single-vision lenses and were monitored for 3 years. [117] Progressive addition lenses had a modest, although statistically significant, treatment impact of 0.20 D reduction in myopia progression over 3 years (−1.28 D compared to −1.48 D), with most of the benefit occurring in the first year. Axial elongation was modestly reduced; however, the reduction was regarded as clinically insignificant. Results from subsequent analyses revealed a larger benefit among children with greater near esophoria and accommodative lag, prompting further focused investigations. [118]

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Progressive and defocus spectacles:
content: Studies in East Asian populations have consistently confirmed the limited efficacy of progressive addition lenses. Hasebe and colleagues conducted a randomized study of Japanese children (−1.25 to −6.00 D) assigned to either progressive addition lenses or single-vision lenses, which found a modest, though statistically significant, decrease in myopia progression over 2 years associated with progressive addition lens use of approximately 0.20 to 0.30 D. [119] The treatment effect was greater in individuals with greater accommodative latency and near esophoria, underscoring the importance of accommodative dysfunction as a crucial determinant of response.

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Progressive and defocus spectacles:
content: Findings from the Cochrane living network meta-analysis on myopia control in children (updated search February 2024) conclude that multifocal and myopia-specific spectacle lenses significantly decrease myopia progression compared to single-vision spectacles, with defocus-based designs (DIMS, HAL/SAL, DOT) exhibiting greater effects on axial length than traditional progressive addition lenses and bifocals. [115] Nonetheless, spectacle choices generally exhibit marginally lower efficacy than higher-dose atropine or orthokeratology in direct comparisons, but they offer benefits in terms of safety, usability, and acceptance. Findings from a 2025 meta-analysis concentrating on myopia-control spectacle lenses aggregated randomized trials of DIMS, HAL/SAL, DOT, and analogous designs, revealing a pooled reduction of approximately 0.35 D in spherical equivalent refraction progression and about 0.18 mm in axial elongation over 1 to 2 years compared to single vision lenses, equating to relative risk reductions of approximately 45% to 50% for rapid progression. [124] . The data indicated that newer lens types (DIMS, HAL, DOT) outperformed conventional progressive addition lenses in network comparisons and that efficacy was generally greater when therapy commenced at younger ages (≤ 10 years) and persisted for at least 2 to 3 years.

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Lifestyle changes:
content: Environmental and behavioral interventions enhance the effectiveness of optical and pharmacological approaches. Extending outdoor exposure to 90 to 120 minutes daily has been shown to reduce the incidence of myopia and slow its initial progression, presumably via mechanisms related to retinal dopamine secretion and increased light exposure. [12] [125] Minimizing prolonged near-work, increasing working distance, and adhering to the 20-20-20 rule (take a break every 20 minutes by gazing at an object 20 feet away for 20 seconds) may alleviate accommodative strain. [16] School-based programs show significant improvements in visual acuity and a decrease in myopia rates with the introduction of structured outdoor breaks. [126] The World Health Organization guidelines advocate public health strategies that combine environmental interventions with therapeutic interventions to reduce the global prevalence of myopia. [127]

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Management
content: Surgical management of myopia has advanced rapidly in the past 2 decades, and can be broadly classified into laser vision correction at the corneal level or lenticular correction at the crystalline lens level.

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Laser refractive correction or laser vision correction:
content: Laser vision correction is the surgical correction of refractive errors by remodeling the corneal surface using laser ablation. This procedure uses an excimer laser, an argon fluoride dimer with a wavelength of 193 nm. [128] These surface lasers fall in the ultraviolet light wavelength range and have limited tissue penetration. The concept of laser vision correction is based on the fact that 80% of light refraction occurs in the cornea; thus, altering the corneal surface can change the pattern of refraction. [129]

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Laser refractive correction or laser vision correction:
content: Because the cornea has a prolate shape, the corneal periphery is flat, and its center is relatively steep. The aspheric shape of the cornea reduces a considerable number of spherical and chromatic aberrations. With central flattening after laser correction, the cornea assumes an oblate shape, accentuating aberrations and degrading visual quality. Excimer laser platforms have changed substantially over the past 2 decades. Excimer laser delivery systems are available in 3 configurations, including broad beam, scanning slit, and flying spot. Broad-beam and scanning-slit lasers have become obsolete and unavailable on newer platforms. The latest versions of laser machines use a flying-spot delivery system that precisely and rapidly delivers laser energy. [130] [131] Surgical techniques include laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK), photorefractive keratectomy (PRK), and small incision lenticule extraction (SMILE).

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Laser refractive correction or laser vision correction:
content: Lasers can be delivered to the cornea with or without flap creation. LASIK is a corneal refractive surgery that involves the creation of a hinged flap on the corneal surface, followed by excimer-laser ablation to remodel the underlying stroma, therefore permanently correcting refractive errors. In LASIK surgery, a microkeratome or a femtosecond laser is used to create a corneal flap 90 to 160 µm thick. [132] [133] Next, the flap is elevated, and, depending on the refractive error, photoablation of the corneal stroma is performed using excimer lasers; the minimum residual stromal bed is maintained at 250 µm. After ablation, the flap is repositioned, and the procedure is completed. (See Image . Steps of LASIK Eye Surgery).

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Laser refractive correction or laser vision correction:
content: Photorefractive keratectomy is a surface-based refractive technique that removes the corneal epithelium and uses excimer laser ablation to remodel the anterior stroma, facilitating the correction of myopia without forming a corneal flap. The cornea is deepithelialized using 20% alcohol or excimer lasers. Photoablation is performed over the Bowman membrane, followed by the application of 0.02% mitomycin-C for 30 seconds to prevent postsurgical corneal haze. After the procedure, a contact lens is placed to facilitate the growth of the corneal epithelium. Once epithelialization is complete, the contact lens is removed. Photorefractive keratectomy is considered the most favorable technique for maintaining corneal biomechanical integrity. [133]

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Laser refractive correction or laser vision correction:
content: Femtosecond lasers are a newer technology used in refractive surgery for myopia. [134] These lasers achieve the highest precision in corneal tissue cutting, thereby providing the desired plane of separation. These lasers can be used to create a flap, following which excimer lasers can be used for ablation. [135] Alternatively, femtosecond lasers can generate a lenticule within the stroma that can be extracted through a small opening on the corneal surface. This lenticular extraction technique is termed small-incision lenticular extraction. [136] This procedure is a minimally invasive refractive surgical procedure that employs a femtosecond laser to generate and excise an intrastromal lenticule via a diminutive corneal incision, therefore modifying corneal curvature to correct myopia.

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Laser refractive correction or laser vision correction:
content: These lasers can be used to correct myopia from −0.5 D to −14 D if the cornea is stable and biomechanically strong. Because these lasers weaken the cornea, eyes with a subclinically weak architecture can experience adverse effects, including conical protrusion and reduced visual acuity. [137] Photorefractive keratectomy is considered the most favorable method for maintaining the biomechanical integrity and corneal anatomy. LASIK is considered the most biomechanically weakening procedure and should thus be performed with caution. [135] [138]

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Laser refractive correction or laser vision correction:
content: Various intraoperative and postoperative complications may occur. Intraoperative complications in LASIK are mostly related to the flap, including incomplete or free flaps and buttonhole flaps. Postoperative complications can be classified into early- and late-stage complications. Early postoperative complications include diffuse lamellar keratitis, epithelial ingrowth leading to the sterile melting of the flap, and sterile stromal infiltrates. Late postoperative complications included myopic regression, post-PRK haze, and post-LASIK ectasia. [139] [140] Corneal laser techniques do not alter the fundamental axial elongation or reduce the risk of complications associated with excessive myopia. These treatments should be considered only once refractive stability is achieved, generally between the ages of 18 and 21 years. Surgical retinal procedures may be required in pathological myopia for complications including myopic traction maculopathy, foveoschisis, or myopic choroidal neovascularization.

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Lenticular correction of myopia:
content: This procedure involves implanting a biocompatible intraocular lens or replacing the lens. Replacing the crystalline lens with an artificial intraocular lens carries a high risk of posterior-segment complications. Hence, a phakic intraocular lens can be considered for patients in whom keratorefractive procedures are contraindicated.

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Lenticular correction of myopia:
content: Phakic intraocular lens (IOL): Phakic IOLs can be classified by their implantation position as anterior- or posterior-chamber. [141] The phakic IOL in the anterior chamber is angle-supported and implanted in front of the iris; however, this lens can lead to endothelial decompensation and increase intraocular pressure by occluding the outflow system. [142] [143] (See Image. Phakic Intraocular Lens). This lens is obsolete owing to its high complication rates. With the advent of the posterior chamber phakic IOL, other lenses have become available.

content: The posterior chamber phakic IOL, which is placed behind the iris and supported at the sulcus, is widely used. [144] Multiple international companies have developed this lens, demonstrating equivalent efficacy and safety. However, the long-term results depend on an accurate preoperative assessment. The preoperative evaluation includes subjective refraction, white-to-white diameter, and anterior chamber depth. [144]

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Lenticular correction of myopia:
content: The white-to-white diameter is typically measured using a digital caliper. The accuracy of digital calipers far outweighs that of optical biometry. [145] The white-to-white diameter correlates with the appropriate size of the phakic IOL, ensuring it remains stable in the sulcus and prevents postoperative rotation or displacement. An undersized or small-diameter phakic IOL may cause rotation and displacement of the lenses, leading to reduced visual acuity. [145]

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Lenticular correction of myopia:
content: Proper sizing of the phakic IOL is critical to providing adequate vault over the crystalline lens. An oversized or larger diameter of the phakic IOL may produce larger vaults, causing the shallowing of the anterior chamber, eventually leading to angle closure and excessive rubbing of the posterior surface of the iris, resulting in pigment dispersion. [147] The patient's subjective refraction determines the power of the phakic IOL, which can be spherical or toric, depending on the refractive status. Some lenses are designed for implantation in the horizontal meridian, irrespective of their toricity. [145]

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Lenticular correction of myopia:
content: The basic structure of the posterior chamber phakic IOL is uniform across all manufacturers; they are available with or without a central hole. These lenses have plate haptics and a 6 mm central optical zone, with a vault or elevation to prevent contact with the crystalline lens. Multiple holes in these lenses facilitate the flow of aqueous from the posterior chamber to the anterior chamber. The presence of a central hole determines whether a peripheral iris opening should be performed. Lenses without a central hole require peripheral iris opening to prevent any postoperative increase in intraocular pressure. [145] [147] Complications of phakic IOL implantation include cataract formation, pigment dispersion, loss of pupillary sphincters, angle-closure glaucoma, and corneal decompensation. Cataract formation and pupillary sphincter damage are observed with the posterior chamber IOL, whereas corneal decompensation is observed with the anterior chamber phakic IOL. [148]

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Lenticular correction of myopia:
content: Lenticular replacement: Lenticular replacement can be considered for patients with poor keratorefractive dynamics and a low anterior chamber depth. [149] The lens can be replaced with an adequately powered posterior chamber IOL in such cases. This procedure is performed using standard phacoemulsification. The power of the IOL is determined using standard optical biometry, which uses laser interferometry. Three types of IOLs are available: monofocal, bifocal, and trifocal. Trifocal lenses are the most advanced form of intracranial lenses that improve all forms of vision, enabling the patient to be free of spectacles. [150]

title: Myopia -- Treatment / Management -- Lenticular correction of myopia:
content: Lenticular replacement is associated with a high incidence of postoperative complications. Posterior-segment complications, such as retinal detachment, are the most significant limitations of this procedure. With the removal of the crystalline lens, the iris lens diaphragm moves forward, pulling the anterior retina and eventually opening the stretched peripheral retina. Retinal detachment is a severe complication that can lead to permanent vision loss. [151] [152]

title: Myopia -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Pseudomyopia is an essential classification of myopia caused by ciliary spasms that prevent relaxation of the zonules and flattening of the crystalline lens when the point of fixation is far. [153] Pseudomyopia denotes a temporary, reversible increase in myopic refractive error induced by excessive accommodation, rather than genuine structural elongation of the eye. Psuedomyopia generally arises from prolonged close tasks, excessive use of digital devices, emotional strain, or accommodative spasm, resulting in continuous contraction of the ciliary muscle and a transient displacement of the focal point anterior to the retina. [48] Children, adolescents, and young adults are predominantly affected due to their eyes' accommodative capacity. [154] Clinically, patients exhibit fluctuating or occasionally obscured distance vision, ocular strain, headaches, and difficulty relaxing focus after extended near tasks. [153] Cycloplegic refraction differentiates pseudomyopia from genuine myopia by demonstrating a less myopic (or emmetropic) baseline refractive condition when accommodation is completely relaxed. Management emphasizes mitigating near-work strain, promoting regular visual breaks, optimizing working distances, and identifying psychological triggers. In chronic cases, short-term cycloplegic therapy may be used to alleviate accommodative strain. Despite being reversible, undetected pseudomyopia may precede or exacerbate the onset and progression of true myopia, underscoring the importance of early identification and behavioral changes for favorable long-term visual outcomes.

title: Myopia -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis of myopia encompasses conditions that resemble refractive myopia or induce subsequent myopic shifts resulting from structural or metabolic anomalies. A critical distinction is whether the refractive error results from axial elongation, increased optical power, or a temporary index alteration induced by systemic factors. Lenticular myopia frequently contributes to secondary refractive error, particularly in older adults, because early nuclear sclerosis alters the refractive index of the crystalline lens, leading to a gradual myopic shift. [155] This variant of myopia is generally associated with diminished contrast sensitivity, increased glare, and lens opacification, as observed during slit-lamp examination. Metabolic disorders, including uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, can lead to lens edema and alterations in refractive index, resulting in variable myopic refraction that improves with glycemic control. Identifying these etiologies facilitates appropriate care and prevents misdiagnosis of subsequent diseases as primary myopia.

title: Myopia -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Congenital or syndromic disorders should be evaluated, particularly in children with early-onset high myopia or unusual ocular manifestations. Conditions such as Marfan syndrome, Stickler syndrome, and Ehlers–Danlos syndrome can induce axial elongation due to connective tissue irregularities affecting the sclera. These patients may exhibit supplementary ocular characteristics such as ectopia lentis, vitreous anomalies, or progressive retinal atrophy. Posterior lenticonus is a rare condition that occurs in isolation or in association with Alport syndrome. The International Myopia Institute underscores the need to recognize red-flag systemic indicators, such as skeletal anomalies, hypermobility, cleft palate, or auditory impairment, that may indicate an underlying syndromic etiology. [156] In infants, retinal dystrophies such as Leber congenital amaurosis or achromatopsia may also manifest with myopia. Differentiating between congenital, syndromic, and simple myopia requires a comprehensive medical history, a family history, and a focused systemic assessment.

title: Myopia -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Pathologies of the retina or optic nerve may be associated with symptoms that overlap with high myopia or resemble alterations in the myopic fundus. Myopic-appearing slanted discs must be differentiated from congenital optic disc hypoplasia or coloboma, since each condition has unique implications for prognosis and monitoring. Furthermore, peripapillary atrophy observed in moderate to high myopia may mimic early glaucomatous changes, complicating diagnosis. Given that high myopia increases the risk of glaucoma, meticulous assessment of optic nerve morphology, retinal nerve fiber layer thickness, and visual fields is necessary. Ocular coherence tomography imaging aids in distinguishing structural anomalies caused by axial elongation from glaucomatous cupping, which has a characteristic pattern of nerve fiber layer atrophy. [20]

title: Myopia -- Staging
content: Myopia is a continuum of refractive and structural alterations that develop over time, commencing far before the detection of clinical refractive error. The initial phase, commonly termed premyopia, is often present in children who have not yet reached the dioptric criteria for myopia but exhibit a constellation of risk factors (such as above-average axial length for their age, a significant familial predisposition, limited outdoor activity, or early indicators of rapid ocular development), suggesting a substantial probability of future myopia. These children generally have normal visual acuity but display modest biometric characteristics that indicate a deviation from the anticipated trajectory of emmetropization. Identifying premyopia is crucial, since it enables the implementation of preventive measures, including promoting outdoor activities and modifying environmental practices that affect ocular development.

title: Myopia -- Staging
content: The staging of myopia offers a systematic framework for categorizing severity, assessing risk of complications, and directing monitoring. Historically, staging has relied on spherical equivalent refractive error, categorizing low myopia as −0.50 to −3.00 D, moderate myopia as −3.00 to −6.00 D, and high myopia as < −6.00 D. However, refractive error alone does not consistently predict risk because eyes with identical dioptric measurements may exhibit differing axial lengths and posterior segment structures. Current guidelines increasingly endorse staging based on axial length, acknowledging that an axial length ≥ 26.0 mm is the most reliable predictor of long-term complications, including retinal detachment, myopic macular degeneration, and glaucoma. [35] High myopia is diagnosed when the axial length exceeds approximately 26 mm or the refractive error exceeds −6.00 D, and is associated with significant stretching and thinning of the sclera, choroid, and retina.

content: Pathologic myopia denotes a specific phase defined not by refractive error but by the existence of structural degenerative lesions in the posterior pole. The Meta-analyses for Pathologic Myopia (META-PM) classification system is extensively used for the staging of pathologic myopia, encompassing the following categories: [157] Category 1: Tessellated fundus Category 2: Diffuse chorioretinal atrophy Category 3: Patchy atrophy Category 4: Macular atrophy Plus lesions: Lacquer cracks, myopic choroidal neovascularization, Fuch spot

title: Myopia -- Staging
content: Supplementary descriptions encompass lacquer cracks, myopic choroidal neovascularization, and a dome-shaped macula. Ocular coherence tomography imaging is essential for staging, as it reveals subtle structural alterations, such as inner retinal schisis, foveal separation, or early retinal pigment epithelium atrophy, that may not be detectable on ophthalmoscopy. Precise staging is crucial for predicting prognosis and determining appropriate monitoring intervals and treatment strategies. Childhood myopia may be categorized by risk of progression, particularly during the school years, when axial elongation occurs most rapidly.

title: Myopia -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis of myopia is determined primarily by age of onset, progression rate, eventual refractive error, and axial length. Children who develop myopia before age 8 years exhibit a markedly elevated risk of progressing to high myopia, as evidenced by longitudinal studies conducted in East Asia, Europe, and the United States. [34] Results from the COMET study found that the mean age of stabilization is 15 to 16 years, with the majority achieving stabilization by age 24 years. [158] Individuals with later-onset myopia generally exhibit a more gradual progression and a lower ultimate refractive error. The prognosis is more favorable when early intervention is implemented because many optical and pharmacological therapies have shown substantial decreases in axial elongation. Recent research on MiSight, DIMS lenses, and atropine trials demonstrates that early intervention can reduce the lifetime risk of developing severe myopia by inhibiting excessive elongation during critical growth phases. [159]

title: Myopia -- Prognosis
content: High myopia has a less favorable prognosis because it is linked to vision-threatening complications. Results from epidemiological studies indicate that persons with a refractive error of ≤ −6.00 D had a significantly elevated lifetime risk of retinal detachment, glaucoma, and myopic macular degeneration. Risks increase with each incremental diopter of refractive error or millimeter of axial elongation. Individuals with axial lengths exceeding 30 mm may be at up to 40 times greater risk of myopic macular degeneration than those with emmetropic eyes. [55] Once degenerative alterations such as lacquer cracks, staphyloma, or choroidal neovascularization manifest, the visual prognosis becomes uncertain. Myopic macular degeneration is a significant cause of maculopathy. Anti–vascular endothelial growth factor therapy improves outcomes for myopic choroidal neovascularization; however, long-term recurrence and the progression of macular atrophy persist as obstacles. Staphyloma can form as an abnormal outpouching of the posterior globe due to weakness of the scleral-uveal layer. The eye globe tends to elongate in the anteroposterior dimension with thinning of the posterior walls. Unlike coloboma, the staphyloma defect is located laterally to the optic disc.

title: Myopia -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis for adults depends on environmental and occupational factors. In many individuals, myopia remains constant; nonetheless, increased digital device use, extended near labor, and diminished outside exposure have contributed to an increase in adult-onset and adult-progression myopia. [160] Adults with substantial myopia ( > −4.00 D) exhibit an elevated lifetime risk of glaucoma, as population-based studies indicate more pronounced relationships with greater refractive errors. Assessing axial length is beneficial in adults experiencing progressive myopic shifts to distinguish between typical age-related refractive alterations and pathological elongation. Prompt identification of high-risk individuals facilitates prompt monitoring and management to maintain long-term visual function.

title: Myopia -- Complications
content: Amblyopia assessment is critical for the appropriate treatment of myopia in young children. Patients with anisometropia are more likely to develop amblyopia in the eye with the higher refractive error, a condition termed anisometropic amblyopia. Ametropic amblyopia is a condition in which patients’ vision does not improve to 20/20, even after best-corrected visual acuity.

title: Myopia -- Complications
content: The posterior segment plays a critical role in successful management. [161] Posterior-segment lesions can be classified as central or peripheral. The primary goal of lesion identification is to prevent retinal detachment and sudden vision loss. Retinal detachment is a well-documented risk, with individuals exhibiting high myopia facing a lifetime risk that is up to 20 times greater than that of those with emmetropia. High refractive error and a longer axial length are the most significant risk factors for posterior-segment lesions. The retina of patients with myopia stretches posteriorly due to increased axial length, eventually leading to peripheral retinal degeneration and thinning. [162]

title: Myopia -- Complications
content: Certain conditions should be observed and treated to prevent retinal detachment. Tears and holes in the peripheral retina should be followed periodically. A horseshoe tear and percolated holes should be treated with retinal laser therapy to prevent future complications. Atrophic holes can be periodically monitored during the development of subclinical retinal detachment. Lattice and pigmentary degeneration are commonly observed in patients with myopia. These lesions do not require treatment when super-filled holes or tears are present. [163] A regular dilated fundus examination is crucial for persons with moderate-to-high myopia, particularly those who exhibit symptoms such as floaters or flashes. Prophylactic laser therapy may be warranted in specific instances with high-risk lesions.

title: Myopia -- Complications
content: The central retina is critical for visual acuity. Anatomical and functional abnormalities are observed in patients with pathological myopia and myopic macular degeneration. Posterior staphyloma, choroidal neovascular membrane, and foveal retinoschisis are the 3 critical lesions observed in patients with myopia > 10 D. Staphyloma can be observed in the macula or peripapillary region. Posterior extension of the sclera disrupts macular support, leading to stretch maculopathy that may require scleral reinforcement. Choroidal neovascular membranes should be monitored, and any progression may require anti–vascular endothelial growth factor therapy. [164] A macular hole is a rare complication following a history of trivial trauma or traction of the posterior hyaloid over the macula. Other lesions, such as a dome-shaped macula, breaks in the Bruch membrane (lacquer cracks), tessellations, and peripapillary atrophy, are observed and do not require aggressive management. [164]

title: Myopia -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Early diagnosis, prevention, treatment, and education are fundamental components in decreasing the prevalence and advancement of myopia, especially in school-aged children. Education must begin early and include guidance on the importance of regular outdoor exposure, which has been shown to mitigate the onset of myopia by stimulating light-induced dopamine release in the retina. Results from randomized controlled trials conducted in Taiwan and China indicate that structured outdoor activities can attenuate declines in population-level visual acuity. [16] Parents and educators should be informed that increasing outdoor time by just 60 to 120 minutes daily will markedly delay the onset of myopia and curtail its early progression. title: Myopia -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Myopia management requires an understanding of essential principles and potential limitations that affect long-term outcomes, clinical judgment, and patient compliance. Axial length, rather than refractive error alone, is the most dependable biomarker for assessing lifetime risk, directing treatment intensity, and evaluating therapeutic response. Clinicians must acknowledge that early onset, rapid growth, and parental myopia are significant predictors of high myopia, necessitating prompt and continuous intervention. A common pitfall is relying exclusively on single-vision correction, which offers superior clarity but overlooks the biological factors that contribute to axial elongation, potentially allowing preventable progression. Another limitation is the underestimation of the cumulative impact of environmental factors, including restricted outdoor exposure and extended near-work, which must be considered alongside optical or pharmacological interventions.

title: Myopia -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes

Clinicians and optometrists must collaborate to ensure accurate diagnosis, risk assessment, and tailored intervention strategies. Efficient interprofessional communication facilitates the prompt identification of rapid progression and the timely commencement of treatment.

Clinicians must engage families in discussions about the cost-benefit analysis of different treatment options, ensuring a transparent, collaborative decision-making process.
